title: Stacks, Queues, and Deques
summary: Use an array as a stack and as a queue with a head index, answer next-greater questions with a monotonic stack, and keep window maximums in a deque.
intro: A stack hands back the newest item first, and a queue the oldest. JavaScript has neither type, and it doesn't need them: an array is both, as long as you use the right end. The interview patterns come from keeping them in a useful order. A monotonic stack answers "what comes next that's bigger?" for every item in one pass, and a deque keeps the maximum of a sliding window.

steps.title: An array as a stack

example.title: Where the brackets break
example.prompt: Read lines of code and report the first bracket problem in each one: a closer that closes nothing, a closer of the wrong kind, or an opener that is never closed.
example.stdin:
4
f(a[i])
if (x) { y = [1, 2) }
sum((a + b) * c
x = y]
example.output:
f(a[i]) -> ok
if (x) { y = [1, 2) } -> ) at 19 does not match [ at 14
sum((a + b) * c -> ( at 4 is never closed
x = y] -> ] at 6 closes nothing
example.explanation: The stack holds **positions**, not characters, so every message can say where the problem is, and `code[top]` still gives the bracket itself. In `f(a[i])` each closer pops its own opener and the stack ends empty. In the second line, `)` pops the `[` at 14, the wrong kind, so the function returns at once. In `sum((a + b) * c` the inner pair matches but the `(` at 4 is left over, and `open[0]` is the oldest bracket still open. In `x = y]` the stack is empty when `]` arrives.

practice.title: Matching tags
practice.prompt:
Check lines of HTML-style tags and report the first problem in each one. 1. The starter reads `n` lines and splits each one into tags such as `` and ``. 2. In `firstProblem`, push every opening tag onto `open`. A closing tag starts with `` closes ``. 3. For a closing tag, return `TAG closes nothing` when `open` is empty, or `TAG does not match TOP` when the top isn't its opener, where TAG is the closing tag and TOP is `open.at(-1)`. Otherwise pop. 4. After the loop, return `FIRST is never closed` when tags are still open, where FIRST is the oldest one, `open[0]`. Otherwise return `ok`. Input: ```text 4

    • ``` Expected output: ```text -> ok

    ->

    does not match
      • ->
        is never closed
    ->
    closes nothing ```

tests.output:
-> ok

->

does not match
    • ->
      is never closed
      ->
      closes nothing

-> is never closed

-> ok -> does not match

hints: `tag.startsWith("</")` tells a closing tag from an opening one.
Check `open.length === 0` first, so a closing tag with nothing open gets its own message before you compare `open.at(-1)` with `"<" + tag.slice(2)`.
When several tags are left open, report `open[0]`, the bottom of the stack, not the top.

steps.title: Queues with a head index

example.title: Round-robin printer
example.prompt: A printer prints up to 2 pages of the front job each turn, and a job with pages left goes to the back of the line. Read the jobs and print the turn on which each one finishes.
example.output:
memo done on turn 2
menu done on turn 4
flyer done on turn 6
report done on turn 7
example.explanation: The jobs start in input order. `queue[head++]` takes the front job, and a job with pages left is pushed again, so it waits behind everyone already in line. `memo` needs one turn and finishes on turn 2, while `report` needs three turns and finishes last. Whenever the served part passes half the array, `splice(0, head)` drops it and `head` goes back to 0, so the served items never outnumber the waiting ones. Each job is an object, so `job.left -= perTurn` changes the same object that goes back in line.

practice.title: Time slices
practice.prompt:
A processor runs tasks in turns. The front task runs for up to `q` milliseconds, then goes to the back of the line if it isn't done. Print the time at which each task finishes.

1. The starter reads `n` and `q`, then puts the `n` tasks in `queue` in input order, each as `{ name, left }`. The clock starts at 0.
2. While tasks are waiting, take the front one with `queue[head++]` and run it for `Math.min(q, task.left)` ms. Add that to `clock` and take it from `task.left`.
3. If the task has time left, push it to the back. Otherwise print `NAME finished at CLOCK`.
4. Compact the queue whenever `head * 2 > queue.length`.

Input:

```text
3 4
build 10
lint 3
test 6
```

Expected output:

```text
lint finished at 7
test finished at 17
build finished at 19
```

tests.output:
lint finished at 7
test finished at 17
build finished at 19

email finished at 30
backup finished at 80

ls finished at 2
ping finished at 4
cat finished at 5

hints: The loop is the example's: `while (head < queue.length)`, with `queue[head++]` for the front task.
A task with less than `q` ms left runs only for what it needs, so add `Math.min(q, task.left)` to the clock, not `q`.

steps.title: Monotonic stacks

example.title: Next taller building
example.prompt: Read the heights of buildings along a street, from west to east, and print the next taller building to the east of each one.
example.output:
Building 1 (40 m): next taller is building 4 (55 m)
Building 2 (25 m): next taller is building 3 (30 m)
Building 3 (30 m): next taller is building 4 (55 m)
Building 4 (55 m): next taller is building 7 (60 m)
Building 5 (35 m): next taller is building 6 (45 m)
Building 6 (45 m): next taller is building 7 (60 m)
Building 7 (60 m): none taller to the east
Building 8 (20 m): none taller to the east
example.explanation: Building 2 (25) waits only until building 3 (30) pops it. Then 55 pops 30 and 40, answering both with building 4, and 60 pops 45 and 55. Buildings 7 and 8 are still on the stack at the end, so they keep -1. This version stores the index `i` as the answer instead of a height, so the output can give both the building's number, `j + 1`, and its height, `heights[j]`.

practice.title: Next price drop
practice.prompt:
For each day's price, find the next later price that is strictly lower, or -1 when no drop comes.

1. The starter reads one line of prices and fills `drop` with -1.
2. Keep a stack of indexes still waiting, their prices going **up** from bottom to top.
3. For each price, pop every waiting index whose price is higher, and set its answer to the current price. An equal price is not a drop, so it keeps waiting.
4. Push the current index. The starter prints the answers on one line.

Input:

```text
8 4 6 6 2 3 5 1
```

Expected output:

```text
4 2 2 2 1 1 1 -1
```
hints: The loop is the example's with the comparison flipped: pop while `prices[stack.at(-1)] > prices[i]`.
Use `>`, not `>=`, so an equal price keeps waiting.
Store the price itself, `drop[stack.pop()] = prices[i]`, not its index.

steps.title: A deque for window extremes

example.title: Peak load per window
example.prompt: Read a window size and a server's load for each minute, then print the peak load in every window of k minutes.
example.output:
Minutes 1-3: peak 9
Minutes 2-4: peak 9
Minutes 3-5: peak 7
Minutes 4-6: peak 7
Minutes 5-7: peak 7
Minutes 6-8: peak 6
example.explanation: When 9 arrives it pops 5 from the back, since 5 can never beat 9 in a later window. The second 7 pops the first one: they tie, and the later one stays in the window longer. At minute 5 the window is minutes 3 to 5, so the 9 from minute 2 has slid out. `head` moves past it, and the 7 from minute 5 becomes the front. The indexes in front of `head` stay in the array but are never read again.

practice.title: Cheapest fare per window
practice.prompt:
Find the cheapest fare in every window of k days.

1. The starter reads `k` from the first line and the fares from the second.
2. Keep indexes in `dq` with their fares going **up** from front to back: before adding `i`, pop from the back every index whose fare is not smaller than `fares[i]`.
3. Move `head` on when the front index slides out of the window.
4. Once a window is full, add the fare at the front to `lows`. The starter prints them on one line.

Input:

```text
3
5 1 6 7 8 2 4
```

Expected output:

```text
1 1 6 2 2
```
hints: This is the example's loop with the comparison flipped: pop while `fares[dq.at(-1)] >= fares[i]`.
The front slides out when `dq[head] <= i - k`.
A window is full from `i = k - 1` on.

recap:
- An array is a stack: `push` adds, `pop` takes the newest, and `at(-1)` peeks, all in O(1). An empty array gives `undefined`, so check `length > 0` first.
- To match brackets or tags, push openers and pop on closers. The stack must end empty.
- `shift()` is O(n). A queue is an array plus a `head` index, and `queue[head++]` takes the front in O(1).
- Compact a long-running queue with `queue.splice(0, head)` once `head * 2 > queue.length`.
- A monotonic stack of indexes answers "the next bigger item" for every index in O(n), because each index is pushed and popped at most once.
- A deque of indexes with values going down keeps every window's maximum at the front. In JavaScript, `push` and `pop` work the back and a `head` index is the front. Flip the comparison for the minimum.
